title: Vietnam's Rabies Crisis: Why Health Experts Are Pushing to End the Dog Meat Trade by 2030
excerpt: A 160% spike in rabies deaths and unregulated dog trafficking are forcing Vietnam's government to confront the public health crisis behind the meat trade. New data shows 95% of Vietnamese support ending it.
body_html:
The Bottom Line

Vietnam is experiencing a 160% surge in human rabies deaths—29 fatalities year-to-date in 2026—directly linked to the unregulated dog and cat meat trade. In January 2026, Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment unveiled a roadmap to eliminate the trade by 2030, backed by a startling consensus: 95% of Vietnamese oppose it. The question is no longer *if* Vietnam will phase out the trade, but *how fast*.

Key Findings

Rabies Epidemic Tied to Uncontrolled Dog Trafficking

A March 2026 directive from Prime Minister Phạm Minh Chính strengthened rabies prevention protocols after documented cases revealed a critical vulnerability: dogs trafficked across provinces lack vaccination records and quarantine certificates, creating disease corridors that bypass every legal safeguard. The scale is staggering—approximately 1 million dogs are trafficked annually, often transported over 1,200 kilometers in inhumane conditions. When animals arrive at slaughter facilities dehydrated, injured, or already sick, the meat itself becomes contaminated with pathogens.

Vietnam's existing Law on Animal Health and Law on Livestock Production contain quarantine requirements that are routinely ignored—a regulatory vacuum that public health officials can no longer tolerate.

Government Launches 2030 Phase-Out Roadmap With International Support

At the Third Technical Meeting of the Companion Animals Technical Working Group on January 27, 2026, Vietnam's Ministry of Agriculture and Environment outlined a concrete five-year strategy to reduce and eliminate the dog and cat meat trade. FOUR PAWS presented a detailed roadmap integrating rabies elimination with economic support for farmers transitioning out of the trade. This is not rhetoric—it's policy infrastructure. Nearly 1,200 dog meat farms have already ceased operations to receive government financial support, accelerating the timeline ahead of the 2027 target.

The roadmap explicitly addresses the veterinary staffing shortages and interprovincial transport loopholes that have allowed disease spread—shifting enforcement from reactive to preventive.

95% of Vietnamese Support a Ban—Yet Enforcement Remains Fragmented

The data is unambiguous. A 2021 survey found 95% of Vietnamese respondents support ending the dog meat trade—a supermajority that dwarfs support for most policy interventions. More recent polling shows 64% back a consumption ban, 68% support banning the trade itself, and 71% favor banning both consumption and trade of cat meat. Yet enforcement remains uneven—no national ban exists as of early 2026, and awareness-raising efforts at district and commune levels remain minimal. This gap between public will and legislative action is the lever for change.

Disease Contamination: 75% of Vietnamese Aware, Yet Sick Animals Still Trafficked

A concerning gap exists between public awareness and market practice: 75% of the Vietnamese population knows that disease-infected animals are being slaughtered and sold, yet infected dogs continue to move across provinces unchecked. The meat is captured using poisoned bait, tasers, and iron pincers, then transported in severe conditions—crammed into small cages on multi-day journeys without adequate food, water, or rest. 88% of survey respondents believe consuming dog meat presents a health risk due to these conditions. Beyond rabies, dog meat has been linked to regional outbreaks of trichinosis and cholera—pathogens that respect no border.

Pet Theft Networks: 5,200+ Dogs Stolen in Single Gia Lai Investigation

In February 2026, police in Gia Lai Province arrested six suspects who had stolen over 5,200 companion dogs (52 metric tons) between 2025 and 2026. The organized ring operated systematically, stealing 20 dogs per night and generating 2.6 billion Vietnamese Đồng in illegal proceeds. These are not isolated incidents—nearly 10,000 dogs and cats were stolen across Vietnam between late 2022 and 2024, representing a public safety and criminal justice crisis alongside the animal welfare emergency.

Also Worth Noting

  • Vietnam's National Assembly Releases Animal Welfare Guidance — A new parliamentary handbook provides delegates with frameworks to strengthen companion animal protections, signaling institutional momentum.
  • International Pressure: Los Angeles Links Sister City Status to Dog Meat Ban — In April 2025, LA City Council proposed conditional sister city recognition with Hanoi, contingent on Vietnam ending the trade.
  • Laws For Paws Vietnam Rescues 800+ At-Risk Dogs — Local volunteer networks have rehabilitated nearly 700 dogs and rehomed 600+ by early 2026, disrupting trafficking supply chains from the ground.
  • Economic Transition: Livelihoods Support Built Into 2030 Roadmap — The government's phase-out plan includes financial assistance for farmers switching trades, addressing the economic dependency that has kept the system alive.
  • Regional Consumption Declining in Key Markets — Dog meat shops in Hà Nội districts like Nhật Tân report declining foot traffic and store closures as urban consumer preferences shift toward pet ownership.

Take Action: Sign the petition to support Vietnam's roadmap toward eliminating the dog meat trade by 2030. Your signature strengthens the hand of the 95% of Vietnamese already calling for change.

Nearly 1,200 dog farms have already voluntarily stopped operations for government financial support.
